technology.flexibus.introduction: FlexiBUS provides a serial connection between a host and its peripherals. Identification is supported: @3. Devices describe their identity and power needs before normal operation.

The interface is available to independent manufacturers. Compatibility commitments depend on implementing the published contracts, including the keyboard standard @45; discovery alone does not qualify a new device class.

Each port connects to one device over separate transmit and receive pairs. Supported raw rates are @14 and @15 bps; the port starts at @16 bps. Cable, power and attachment rules remain part of electrical qualification.
Messages identify their class, request and payload length. A payload is limited to @26 bytes. Framing, error detection and explicit receiver readiness bound each exchange.
Device commands cover discovery, reset, input, printing and disk operations. Request identity and session state prevent a retry from repeating an operation whose outcome is uncertain.
Qualification must exercise the host and peripheral together, including service delays, backpressure and fault recovery. The checks below are requirements, not recorded passing results.

technology.plug_and_execute.introduction: An expansion board carries identification and driver code in ROM so the host can configure it automatically. Manual configuration switches are required: @1. Reserved connector capacity permits later extensions without promising that every future board is already supported.

technology.xip_rom_platform.introduction: The execution model is @1. Keeping suitable code and constants in ROM reduces RAM demand, while replaceable cartridges provide a controlled distribution and upgrade path.

technology.logix_digital_video.introduction: The link carries @1 data bits over a cable with @2. Separate clock, control and synchronisation signals accompany the pixel data.

The host negotiates a raster the monitor can actually display before enabling the picture. Capability failures require an explicit safe profile; connection alone does not establish a supported resolution.
Raster @29 displays @30 by @31 active pixels at @32 MHz. The total pixel and line counts below include blanking.
Raster @35 displays @36 by @37 active pixels at @38 MHz. The total pixel and line counts below include blanking.
Raster @41 displays @42 by @43 active pixels at @44 MHz. Its frame rate is @48 Hz and interlacing is enabled: @49.
Logical image sizes and palette indices must be mapped explicitly to the selected output. A wider logical mode cannot be forced onto a monitor that lacks the required raster.

technology.logix_tui_standard.introduction: Applications share controls and editing conventions rather than defining incompatible interfaces. System clipboard support is enabled: @12. The same conventions cover the listed application classes.
The portable API is @20 and display services use @21. Layout, editing, input and lifecycle services provide the same meanings across the supported hosts.
Each application owns its interface state. Host differences affect resource and lifecycle capabilities, but do not silently change the meaning of the common API.

technology.logix_tui_keyboard_standard.introduction: Native Logix applications use a common command vocabulary. Terminal compatibility profiles remain explicit so an editing shortcut cannot silently become a process-control command.
Navigation commands move the caret or selection by a defined unit. Shift extends the same movement; selection clearing respects active menus and dialogs. For example, character movement uses @8.
Copy, cut, paste and undo have shared logical commands. Keyboard aliases retain the same command scope. Copy uses @38, while paste uses @44.
Document commands cover creation, opening, saving, search and closure. Save uses @65; the application must still report errors and protect modified work.
Focus and lifecycle commands are dispatched to the appropriate control, dialog, application or system. Cooperative cancellation uses @128; it does not imply forced termination.

technology.logix_tui_keyboard_standard.chapter_name: Editing behaviour and ownership of state
technology.logix_tui_keyboard_standard.introduction: Shared behaviour defines selection boundaries, clipboard failure handling, saving and context-sensitive keys. Resource limits and the single-foreground Aurelia model still apply.
Terminal sessions may assign control keys to interrupt, suspend or line editing. These are explicit terminal profiles, separate from the native TUI keymap. Terminal copy uses @158.
The keyboard is @171 and transport uses @172. Events must preserve key identity and modifiers; byte-terminal fallbacks must advertise limitations instead of promising ambiguous shortcuts.

technology.abacus_sparse_model.introduction: Abacus stores populated cells using @1 and represents their contents with @2. This avoids the memory cost of reserving storage for every possible cell on an 8-bit computer.

technology.pulse_notebook_model.introduction: Pulse organises code as @1. Its basic types and control-flow tools support interactive work without changing the ownership rules for documents.
Standalone Pulse works on closed documents under exclusive writer ownership. Embedded execution is a separate versioned feature; introducing it does not extend older editions automatically.

technology.aion_c_portability_framework.introduction: The framework targets @1 and @2. Applications share source code, libraries and API meanings; moving between instruction sets still requires a target-specific build.
Separate shared application logic from host adapters and target build outputs. The three build profiles make the base Aurelia budget, Aurelia+ requirements and native Artemis target explicit.

Portability work must address instruction sets, OS interfaces, memory ownership and file encoding. More capable hardware does not automatically make its application features available on an older host.

technology.era1_isa.introduction: ERAv1 has a @1-bit system bus, @2 and @4. The prefetch buffer holds @8 words. Conditional execution and the two abort classes are part of the instruction contract.

technology.artemis_memory_model.introduction: Artemis separates @1-bit virtual addresses from @2-bit physical addresses. Pages contain @7 bytes, and the design avoids allocating a flat table for the entire virtual space.
The translation cache has @9 entries and is @10. Software controls replacement and preserves the access, reference and dirty information needed by the kernel.

Only allocated virtual mappings require backing records. The per-record planning budget is @22 bytes; it is not a measured total for a process. Fault handling must preserve memory ownership and restart semantics.
Translation uses a conservative wait/ready interface. Faster internal clocks are an option to qualify, not a promise that DRAM access or software refill becomes free.
A module and its selected bank each transfer @42 bits. Banks require independent rank selection, refresh, byte writes and a qualified electrical interface.

Populate capacity banks with matched full-width modules and distinguish installed capacity from the CPU address-space limit. The current parity-bit count is @67; a later parity design requires its own BOM.

technology.aionix_os_model.introduction: AIONix follows @1 with a minimum RAM design target of @2 KB. ROM-backed executables are supported: @3. The process-count example is @5, not an unrestricted concurrency guarantee.
Normal operating-system interfaces mediate application access to files and devices. Initial networking support is @12, and symbolic-link support remains explicitly limited.

technology.aionix_os_model.chapter_name: ABI, memory protection and portable applications
technology.aionix_os_model.introduction: The C ABI is stable within the ERA target. Demand paging is enabled: @25. Portable source services use @32; this does not establish Z80 binary compatibility.

technology.cpm80_virtual_peripheral_brid.introduction: Qualified CP/M binaries run on a Z80 guest while the ERA host supplies services. The bridge preserves documented interfaces; it is not native execution of Z80 instructions on ERA.
Guest stubs marshal bounded requests to a privileged host driver. The mailbox identifies requests, buffers and completion status; every guest buffer must be validated before the host uses it.
The guest sees the surface and services actually exposed by the bridge. Direct hardware access and undocumented software behaviour remain outside the guaranteed compatibility scope.

technology.logix_tcpip_lan.chapter_name: Portable networking over a local link
technology.logix_tcpip_lan.introduction: The network protocol is @1, carried by @2. Keeping the internet protocols above the local link permits future physical links to preserve higher-level software interfaces.

technology.logix_lan100_link.introduction: Stations connect through an active hub over @4 using @3. The hub grants one transmitter at a time; this baseline is a shared network rather than independent switched links.

Supported raw rates are @14, @15, @16 and @17 kbit/s. Startup and fallback use @18 kbit/s. Every admitted station shares the same negotiated rate, and host qualification constrains advertised capabilities.

The hub selects the highest rate supported by every admitted station and link. Changes are coordinated through acknowledgements, a quiet switch interval and test frames; failures return to the startup rate.
Adapters offload framing and buffer complete frames. The local packet RAM target is @51 bytes, separate from host RAM. Receiver credit controls admission of complete frames before transmission.
Timing, buffer limits, recovery and mixed-host throughput require measurement. The qualification checks below must pass before advertised rates become delivery claims.

technology.bpi_relational_database.introduction: BPI applications share a relational database so accounting, receivables, payables, inventory and payroll can use a consistent data foundation. The specification defines that architecture without asserting unrecorded capacity or throughput.

technology.aurelia_memory_model.introduction: The CPU addresses @1 KB at once, with @2 KB pages. Fixed lower RAM is @3 KB, the switchable window is @4 KB and common system RAM is @5 KB. Additional physical RAM does not widen the CPU logical address space.

technology.aurelia_memory_model.chapter_name: CP/M application boundary and service dispatch
technology.aurelia_memory_model.introduction: The published top of application memory must remain writable throughout program execution. System-call dispatch temporarily changes mappings only after moving into common memory, then restores the caller view.

With @29 KB installed, the application range is @30–@31 and contains @34 bytes. The @36 KB profile exposes @41 bytes. These profiles reserve workspace before launch rather than shrinking a running program.

The controller has @44 transfer contexts but @45 active transfer engine. Destination addresses and lengths use @46 and @47 bits respectively. Physical bank selection must remain stable for an active transfer.
System DRAM refresh runs independently of CPU execution: @59. It covers all installed banks: @60. Display DRAM and sprite SRAM have separate ownership and refresh requirements.
The normal base-system view contains @70 KB of contiguous lower RAM and @69 KB of common system RAM. Temporary overlays preserve hidden RAM while exposing ROM and display windows.
The expansion profile contains @88 KB of installed RAM, including @90 KB of contiguous lower RAM. The expansion fills the normal B000–EFFF range; system overlays remain temporary.
Aurelia+ exposes @105 KB of contiguous lower RAM and @104 KB of common system RAM. The normal application map and the temporary service overlays have distinct roles.

technology.logix_c_api.introduction: Version @1 defines shared function meanings, ownership and errors. Source compatibility spans Z80 and ERA, while each target retains its own binary ABI.

technology.logix_c_api.chapter_name: Errors, memory ownership and host adapters
technology.logix_c_api.introduction: Applications receive defined errors and provide bounded buffers. Platform adapters hide host-specific display, file, memory, timing and lifecycle services; persistent files never contain raw pointers.
Both hosts use the @26 target. Applications query usable display dimensions and capabilities rather than choosing behaviour from the computer name.
Artemis and Artemis PRO use the @34 target. Native applications discover supported text modes through the display API while keeping the shared source-level contract.

The AIONix2 system-ROM baseline retains a documented execution path for ERA applications. Individual editions still require qualification; internal system ROM does not imply external application cartridges.

technology.logix_display_api.introduction: Applications enumerate and test usable modes before changing the display. The API reports the configuration actually selected; a named mode is not guaranteed to exist on every host.

Descriptors report geometry, pixel format, buffering, sprites and output scaling. The host intersects controller, monitor and memory capabilities; failures use defined results rather than an unsafe display mode.

Applications draw through context, clipping, bitmap and presentation operations instead of assuming native video RAM layout. Optional compatibility canvases and richer text modes must be discovered explicitly.
Text and bitmap modes reuse display memory. Mode changes validate resources, quiesce drawing and rebuild the layout while preserving application document state outside the screen buffer.

technology.logix_c_target_contract.introduction: Both compilers implement a documented contemporary C subset. Shared structures, function pointers and library contracts support portability without assuming later language standards.
Target @7 uses @9-bit characters, @10-bit short integers, @11-bit integers and @12-bit long integers. Ordinary data pointers contain @13 bits.
Target @14 uses @16-bit characters, @17-bit short integers, @18-bit integers and @19-bit long integers. Ordinary data pointers contain @20 bits.

Each target must define layout, calling conventions and numeric behaviour. Portability requires explicit serialization and bounded platform adapters rather than identical pointer or structure representations.

technology.nmos_3um.introduction: This fabrication technology defines a process family. Geometry and lithography parameters describe its baseline; logic, memories and analog circuits still require separate recipes and qualification.

technology.nmos_275um.introduction: This fabrication technology defines a process family. Geometry and lithography parameters describe its baseline; logic, memories and analog circuits still require separate recipes and qualification.

technology.nmos_2um.introduction: This fabrication technology defines a process family. Geometry and lithography parameters describe its baseline; logic, memories and analog circuits still require separate recipes and qualification.

technology.nmos_15um.introduction: This fabrication technology defines a process family. Geometry and lithography parameters describe its baseline; logic, memories and analog circuits still require separate recipes and qualification.

technology.abacus_formatted_tables.introduction: Formatted tables coexist with sparse worksheet tabs. Stable row and column identities preserve meaning through sorting and filtering; the format is an independent Abacus design.
Storage is divided into row groups, column chunks and pages. Queries read required columns and skip blocks only when conservative metadata proves that no row can match.
Calculated columns use side-effect-free expressions with explicit dependencies. Scalar lookup and multi-row joins have different cardinality rules; the launch SQL subset is read-only.

technology.abacus_formatted_tables.chapter_name: Launch schema and later nested values
technology.abacus_formatted_tables.introduction: Launch tables use flat typed columns. Nested arrays, maps and structures remain a later extension with explicit resource and semantic limits, not an implied launch capability.

technology.abacus_embedded_pulse.introduction: Embedded Pulse runs inside Abacus under the host document API. The open document has one writer; standalone offline access remains a separate mode.

Scripts may perform explicit document edits, but ordinary formula evaluation remains side-effect-free. Cancellation, undo and recalculation boundaries protect consistency without duplicating the whole document.

technology.scanline_palette_list.introduction: The list begins at @1 and occupies @2 bytes. Each record uses @3 bytes, allowing @4 entries. The record format encodes a scanline delta and a palette-register write.
List positions refer to physical output scanlines. Replay restarts from a restored base palette each frame; CPU updates occur only while the single list buffer is safe to modify.
Palette commands use an opt-in blanking-window extension on the existing control pair. Complete validated batches commit before active pixels; the per-line write budget requires qualification.
Test worst-case timing, record limits, memory contention and recovery together. A large total list does not permit an unlimited number of writes during one horizontal blank.

technology.flexibus_pointing_device.introduction: The pointing device uses @1 with versioned class discovery and bounded reports. Motion and button transitions must survive retry without being applied twice.
Buttons and independent rollers have defined actions. Host drivers preserve the common protocol across architectures and retain the bus attachment restrictions.

technology.logix_tui_mouse.introduction: The mouse extension builds on @1 and uses @2. Standard controls receive semantic actions while retaining keyboard operation, clipping, capture and modal behaviour.

Existing applications gain pointer support only through compatible replaceable services or a qualified relink. Input remains owned by the active context, and a hardware cursor consumes an existing sprite resource.
Test both updated pointer interaction and unchanged keyboard-only use. Rendering, capture, removal and ABI compatibility must work across the supported layouts.

technology.artemis_professional_graphics.introduction: Professional graphics uses @1 for capability discovery. The colour command display and monochrome CAD canvas have independent resources and explicit input focus.
The accelerator supports bounded drawing operations while vector geometry remains authoritative. Damage redraw, line quality and memory limits govern the rendering strategy.
Visible display reads consume bandwidth before host drawing or acceleration is considered. Qualify worst-case arbitration and provide a capability-based software development path.

technology.era2_architecture.introduction: ERA² builds on @1 with a @2-bit system bus and @3-bit virtual addresses. Physical addresses contain @4 bits, spanning @5 GiB; installed board memory remains a separate limit.
The instruction-cache target is @8 bytes. External cache options are @9 and @10 KB, but neither external cache nor an FPU is automatically included in the system BOM.

The translation cache targets @12 entries with associativity @13 and address-space identifiers enabled: @14. Stronger restart semantics support the intended paging model without claiming that ERAv1 lacked aborts.
Measure improvement on named workloads and configurations. Packaging, timing, coherency, translation and write buffering remain design decisions or qualification gates.

Conditional and speculative work must not commit effects that the architectural instruction stream did not perform. Fault reporting distinguishes restartable translation failures from external effects that cannot be undone.
The baseline allocation is @42 bytes, with @43 bytes under evaluation. Cache layout, refill policy and the transistor envelope must be checked against real workload traces.

The controller uses explicit waits and bounded ownership. At the 12 MHz planning point, the first word takes @49 clocks and a same-row following word takes @50; these are engineering budgets with stated exclusions.
Instruction visibility and DMA synchronization must be explicit. The candidate write buffer has @63 entries and is conditional on preserving ordering, error reporting and restart semantics.

technology.aurelia_video_profile.chapter_name: Mode discovery and shared video memory
technology.aurelia_video_profile.introduction: The display link is @1 and applications use @2. Text and bitmap allocations are mutually exclusive uses of display DRAM, while sprites retain their separate SRAM.
Mode @8 provides @9 columns by @10 rows, with @13 by @14 pixel glyphs. One shared font serves both text pages; the configurations list exact memory allocations with and without sprites.
Mode @39 provides @40 columns by @41 rows, with @44 by @45 pixel glyphs. Monitor capability must support the wider raster; memory allocations remain explicit for each page and sprite combination.
Mode @70 uses @73 bit per pixel and @74 bytes per framebuffer. Its configurations expose one bitmap page while keeping optional sprites in separate SRAM.
Mode @87 uses @90 bits per pixel and @91 bytes per framebuffer. The listed allocations do not promise a second complete background page.
Mode @104 uses @107 bit per pixel and @108 bytes per framebuffer. Two background pages fit when the listed double-buffered configuration is selected.
Mode @129 uses @132 bits per pixel and @133 bytes per framebuffer. It trades vertical resolution for a wider pixel index within the same display RAM budget.
Mode @146 uses @149 bits per pixel and @150 bytes per framebuffer. The smaller page permits the listed one-page and two-page configurations.
Mode @171 uses @174 bits per pixel and @175 bytes per framebuffer. This is the explicit compatibility mode; scaling and available sprites still follow the common display contracts.

technology.logix_sprite_system.introduction: Profile 1 supports @1 sprites, with up to @2 on a scanline. Each is @3 by @4 pixels at @5 bits per pixel; palette index @7 is transparent.
Patterns consume @13 bytes and descriptors consume @16 bytes within @17 bytes of dedicated SRAM. Spare storage is @18 bytes. Descriptor double buffering does not imply two complete pattern sets.
Profile 2 supports @21 sprites, with up to @22 on a scanline. Each is @23 by @24 pixels at @25 bits per pixel; palette index @27 is transparent.
Patterns consume @33 bytes and the descriptor allocation reserves @36 bytes within @37 bytes of SRAM. The @38 spare bytes and the descriptor-padding note make the reservation explicit.

technology.aion_fab_process_control.introduction: A wafer history connects material, equipment, recipe and electrical results. Process measurements and corrective action distinguish random defects from systematic drift.
Engineering activity and released manufacture have different acceptance requirements. Yield reporting keeps wafer, die, package and saleable-output measures separate.

technology.aion_memory_test.introduction: ROM, SRAM and DRAM need different electrical tests. Qualification spans the specified operating conditions and retains evidence that can be traced to lots and failures.

Redundancy can improve accepted output only on revisions that implement it. After supported repair, the complete device must be tested again; unrepaired launch designs receive no assumed repair benefit.
